title: Cells, tissues and organs
keyIdea: Your body is built in levels. Cells are the tiny building blocks, too small to see without a microscope. A group of similar cells doing one job is a tissue, like muscle tissue. Different tissues working together make an organ, like the stomach or the heart. Organs work together in an organ system, like the circulatory system, and all the systems together make your body.
familyTip: Build the levels with Lego or pasta: one brick is a cell, a row of the same bricks is a tissue, a few different rows stuck together are an organ, and a set of organs is a system. Then name an organ at dinner (stomach, heart, lungs) and ask which system it belongs to.

visual.caption: Which level is it? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: zoom from the body to one cell, build tissues from similar cells, build the stomach from tissues, sort organs into systems and order the levels.

kid: Your body is made of cells. Cells are tiny. Most are far too small to see with just your eyes. You need a microscope to see them.
Lots of similar cells working together make a tissue. Muscle cells make muscle tissue, which can squeeze. Nerve cells make nerve tissue, which carries messages.
Different tissues work together to make an organ. Your stomach has muscle tissue to churn food, lining tissue to make juices, and nerve tissue to send messages. So an organ is bigger than a tissue.
Organs work in teams called organ systems. The heart and blood vessels make the circulatory system. The stomach and intestines are in the digestive system. All the systems together make you!
adult: Ages 7 to 9. Living things are built in levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems and the whole organism. England's KS3 biology names this as 'the hierarchical organisation of multicellular organisms'. Many primary schemes and BBC Bitesize start it earlier. Key words: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism, microscope.

Make the levels with your hands. One Lego brick is a cell. A row of matching bricks is a tissue. A few different rows clipped together make an organ, and a set of those is a system. Ask your child to point to each level and say what it is made of.

Common mistakes: thinking cells are big enough to see; thinking a tissue is any mix of cells, not a group of similar cells with one job; thinking an organ has only one tissue; mixing up which is bigger, tissue or organ; and putting an organ in the wrong system, such as the heart in the breathing system because it sits by the lungs. Be careful to say 'similar cells', since real tissues also hold a few helper cells.

In the lab your child zooms from the body to the circulatory system, the heart, heart muscle and one muscle cell. They build muscle and then nerve tissue from a tray of mixed cells, and build the stomach from muscle, lining and nerve tissue (bone does not fit). Then they sort six organs into three systems and put the five levels in order of size.

choices: A group of similar cells doing one job
practice.hint: Think of muscle tissue. What kind of cells is it made of?
practice.explain: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on one job, like muscle cells making muscle tissue.

practice.prompt: An organ is made of {a} kinds of tissue. You add {b} more kinds of tissue to your model. How many kinds of tissue does the model have now?
practice.hint: Organs are made of several tissues. Add the new kinds to the ones you had.
practice.explain: {a} kinds plus {b} more kinds makes {=a+b} kinds of tissue, all working together in one organ.

practice.prompt: A tissue model needs {a} cells in each row and has {b} rows. How many cells are in the tissue?
practice.hint: Count the cells in one row, then count the rows. Multiply.
practice.explain: {a} cells in each of {b} rows: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} cells. A real tissue has millions of cells.

practice.prompt: Which list goes from smallest to biggest?
practice.hint: What is a tissue made of? Start with that.
practice.explain: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs and organs make organ systems, so the order is cell, tissue, organ, organ system.

practice.prompt: Which system is the stomach part of?
practice.hint: What does the stomach do with your food?
practice.explain: The stomach breaks down food, so it is part of the digestive system, with the intestines.

pool.prompt: Can you see one of your skin cells with just your eyes?
choices: Yes, it is as big as a freckle
pool.hint: Scientists use a special tool to look at cells. Why?
pool.explain: Most cells are far too small to see with your eyes. A microscope makes them look big enough to see.

pool.prompt: Muscle tissue, lining tissue and nerve tissue work together in the stomach. So the stomach is…
pool.hint: What do we call several different tissues working together?
pool.explain: Different tissues working together make an organ. The stomach is an organ.

pool.prompt: Mia says a tissue is bigger than an organ. Is she right?
choices: No, an organ is made of tissues, so it is bigger
pool.hint: Which one is made of the other?
pool.explain: An organ is built from several tissues, so the organ is bigger than any one of its tissues.

pool.prompt: An organ system has {a} organs. Scientists add {b} more organs that work in the same system. How many organs are in the system now?
pool.hint: Add the new organs to the ones already in the system.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} organs, all working together in one organ system.

pool.prompt: Which system are the heart and blood vessels part of?
pool.hint: The heart pumps blood. Which system moves blood round the body?
pool.explain: The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels. Together they are the circulatory system.

pool.prompt: Sam puts a nerve cell into his muscle tissue model. What is wrong?
choices: A tissue is made of similar cells, so muscle tissue needs muscle cells
pool.hint: What kind of cells does muscle tissue need?
pool.explain: Muscle tissue is a group of similar cells, muscle cells, that all squeeze. A nerve cell belongs in nerve tissue.

pool.prompt: A model has {a} rows of {b} cells. How many cells is that?
pool.hint: Multiply the number of rows by the cells in each row.
pool.explain: {a} rows of {b} cells: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} cells in the model tissue.

pool.hint: What do all the systems make together?
pool.explain: All the organ systems work together to make the whole body, the biggest level.

pool.prompt: Which pair are both in the breathing system?
pool.hint: Which organs carry and take in air?
pool.explain: The windpipe carries air to the lungs, so both are in the breathing system. The heart is in the circulatory system.

pool.prompt: Why does the stomach need muscle tissue?
choices: To squeeze and churn the food
pool.hint: Muscle tissue is good at one job. What is it?
pool.explain: Muscle tissue squeezes. In the stomach it churns food and mixes it with juices.
